claim: EDEM2 stably disulfide-bonded to TXNDC11 is responsible for the first mannose trimming step from M9 to M8B in mammalian glycoprotein ERAD.
source: We previously showed that EDEM2 stably disulfide-bonded to the thioredoxin domain-containing protein TXNDC11 is responsible for the first step (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (George et al., 2020)

claim: Incubation of pyridylamine-labeled M8B with purified EDEM3 alone produced M7 (M7A and M7C), M6, and M5.
source: Incubation of pyridylamine-labeled M8B with purified EDEM3 alone produced M7 (M7A and M7C), M6, and M5.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5D

claim: EDEM1 showed a similar tendency to EDEM3 in producing M7, M6, and M5 from M8B, although much lower amounts of M6 and M5 were produced.
source: EDEM1 showed a similar tendency, although much lower amounts of M6 and M5 were produced.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: EDEM3 is a major α1,2-mannosidase for the second step from M8B in mammalian glycoprotein ERAD.
source: Thus, EDEM3 is a major α1,2-mannosidase for the second step from M8B.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing EDEM3 efficiently converts M8B to M7, M6, and M5

claim: Both EDEM3 and EDEM1 trimmed M8B from a glycoprotein efficiently.
source: Both EDEM3 and EDEM1 trimmed M8B from a glycoprotein efficiently.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7

claim: MAN1B1 is localized in the Golgi apparatus.
source: Our confirmation of the Golgi localization of MAN1B indicates that no other α1,2-mannosidase is required for gpERAD.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: No other α1,2-mannosidase is required for mammalian glycoprotein ERAD besides EDEM2-TXNDC11, EDEM3, and EDEM1.
source: Our confirmation of the Golgi localization of MAN1B indicates that no other α1,2-mannosidase is required for gpERAD. Accordingly, we have established the entire route of oligosaccharide processing and the enzymes responsible.
evidence: Inferred from Golgi localization of MAN1B1 and the ability of EDEM proteins to produce all necessary oligosaccharide structures

claim: TXNDC11 helps EDEM2 to form the disulfide bond between C65 and C408.
source: We concluded that TXNDC11 helps EDEM2 to form the disulfide bond between C65 and C408, which is essential for EDEM2 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by LC/MS/MS/MS data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating disulfide bonding between C65 and C408 only in EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex

claim: The disulfide bond between C65 and C408 is essential for EDEM2 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity.
source: We concluded that TXNDC11 helps EDEM2 to form the disulfide bond between C65 and C408, which is essential for EDEM2 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (George et al., 2020)

claim: C160 and C529 of EDEM1 are critical for EDEM1 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity.
source: Results showed that the mutations C160A and C529A of EDEM1 as well as C82A and C441A of EDEM3 indeed inactivated EDEM1 and EDEM3, respectively, in gpERAD (Figure 2C and D). Thus, the conserved cysteine residues, at which intramolecular disulfide bonding was confirmed in EDEM2, turned out to be critical for EDEM1 and EDEM3 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activities, as expected.
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2C

claim: C82 and C441 of EDEM3 are critical for EDEM3 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity.
source: Results showed that the mutations C160A and C529A of EDEM1 as well as C82A and C441A of EDEM3 indeed inactivated EDEM1 and EDEM3, respectively, in gpERAD (Figure 2C and D). Thus, the conserved cysteine residues, at which intramolecular disulfide bonding was confirmed in EDEM2, turned out to be critical for EDEM1 and EDEM3 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activities, as expected.
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2D

claim: C410 and C457 of EDEM1 are important for the α1,2-mannosidase activity of EDEM1.
source: Results also showed that the mutations C410A and C457A of EDEM1 inactivated the α1,2-mannosidase activity of EDEM1 (Figure 2C), suggesting that C410 and C457 of EDEM1 might form a local disulfide bond to stabilize the MHD of EDEM1.
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2C

claim: C410 and C457 of EDEM1 might form a local disulfide bond to stabilize the MHD of EDEM1.
source: Results also showed that the mutations C410A and C457A of EDEM1 inactivated the α1,2-mannosidase activity of EDEM1 (Figure 2C), suggesting that C410 and C457 of EDEM1 might form a local disulfide bond to stabilize the MHD of EDEM1.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of mutagenesis data and previous structural predictions

claim: Four of eight cysteine residues present in EDEM1 can act as free thiols, while the other four cysteine residues form two disulfide bonds (C160-C529 and C410-C457).
source: In this connection, it was previously suggested that four of eight cysteine residues present in EDEM1 can act as free thiols and may be involved in thiol-dependent interaction with substrates, whereas the other four cysteine residues are in sufficient proximity to form two disulfide bonds (C160-C529 and C410-C457) (Lamriben et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Lamriben et al., 2018)

claim: Cysteine residues outside of the MHD of EDEM1 and EDEM3 are not important for their α1,2-mannosidase activity.
source: In contrast, cysteine residues outside of the MHD of EDEM1 and EDEM3 are not important for their α1,2-mannosidase activity (Figure 2C and D), unlike C558 of EDEM2, which is stably disulfide-bonded to C692 of TXNDC11 (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2C and 2D

claim: C558 of EDEM2 is stably disulfide-bonded to C692 of TXNDC11.
source: In contrast, cysteine residues outside of the MHD of EDEM1 and EDEM3 are not important for their α1,2-mannosidase activity (Figure 2C and D), unlike C558 of EDEM2, which is stably disulfide-bonded to C692 of TXNDC11 (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (George et al., 2020)

claim: MAN1B1 is not colocalized with the ER marker mEGFP-KDEL in HCT116 cells.
source: MAN1B1-mCherry driven by the CMV promoter or CMVshort promoter was not colocalized with mEGFP-KDEL, an ER marker, but was colocalized with mEGFP-Giantin, a Golgi marker, in HCT116 cells (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3

claim: MAN1B1 is colocalized with the Golgi marker mEGFP-Giantin in HCT116 cells.
source: MAN1B1-mCherry driven by the CMV promoter or CMVshort promoter was not colocalized with mEGFP-KDEL, an ER marker, but was colocalized with mEGFP-Giantin, a Golgi marker, in HCT116 cells (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3

claim: MAN1B1 is not colocalized with the ER marker mEGFP-KDEL in HeLa cells.
source: Again, MAN1B1-mCherry driven by the CMV promoter or CMVshort promoter was not colocalized with mEGFP-KDEL but rather with mEGFP-Giantin in HeLa cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: MAN1B1 is colocalized with the Golgi marker mEGFP-Giantin in HeLa cells.
source: Again, MAN1B1-mCherry driven by the CMV promoter or CMVshort promoter was not colocalized with mEGFP-KDEL but rather with mEGFP-Giantin in HeLa cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Some MAN1B1-mCherry highly expressed from the CMV promoter overlapped with Lamp1-mGFP (lysosome marker) in HeLa cells.
source: Interestingly, some MAN1B1-mCherry highly expressed from the CMV promoter overlapped with Lamp1-mGFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), whereas MAN1B1-mCherry never overlapped with mEGFP-KDEL, even after higher expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: MAN1B1-mCherry never overlapped with mEGFP-KDEL, even after higher expression in HeLa cells.
source: Interestingly, some MAN1B1-mCherry highly expressed from the CMV promoter overlapped with Lamp1-mGFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), whereas MAN1B1-mCherry never overlapped with mEGFP-KDEL, even after higher expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: MAN1B1-mediated mannose trimming cannot participate in gpERAD, which occurs in the ER.
source: Thus, MAN1B1-mediated mannose trimming cannot participate in gpERAD, the events in the ER.
evidence: Inferred from localization data showing MAN1B1 is in Golgi, not ER

claim: TXNDC11 is not disulfide-bonded to EDEM1.
source: Simultaneous introduction of 3xFlag-tagged TXNDC11 and 3xFlag-tagged EDEM1 into EDEM1-KO cells or simultaneous introduction of 3xFlag-tagged TXNDC11 and 3xFlag-tagged EDEM3 into EDEM3-KO cells did not change band patterns compared with single introduction of 3xFlag-tagged EDEM1 into EDEM1-KO cells or single introduction of 3xFlag-tagged EDEM3 into EDEM3-KO cells (Figure 4A (a, b)).
evidence: Inferred from non-reducing SDS-PAGE data showing no complex formation between TXNDC11 and EDEM1

claim: TXNDC11 is not disulfide-bonded to EDEM3.
source: Simultaneous introduction of 3xFlag-tagged TXNDC11 and 3xFlag-tagged EDEM1 into EDEM1-KO cells or simultaneous introduction of 3xFlag-tagged TXNDC11 and 3xFlag-tagged EDEM3 into EDEM3-KO cells did not change band patterns compared with single introduction of 3xFlag-tagged EDEM1 into EDEM1-KO cells or single introduction of 3xFlag-tagged EDEM3 into EDEM3-KO cells (Figure 4A (a, b)).
evidence: Inferred from non-reducing SDS-PAGE data showing no complex formation between TXNDC11 and EDEM3

claim: EDEM2 is the main partner of TXNDC11.
source: When any of 3xFlag-tagged EDEM1, EDEM2, and EDEM3 was introduced into WT HCT116 cells, followed by immunoprecipitation with anti-Flag antibody and subsequent immunoblotting using anti-TXNDC11 antibody under reducing and non-reducing conditions, endogenous TXNDC11 was clearly co-immunoprecipitated from cells overexpressing 3xFlag-tagged EDEM2, indicating that EDEM2 is the main partner of TXNDC11 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B

claim: M8B was accumulated in EDEM1,3-DKO cells.
source: M9 was accumulated in EDEM-TKO cells as we described previously (Ninagawa et al., 2015), whereas M8B was accumulated in EDEM1, 3-DKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), as we expected.
evidence: Supported by N-glycan profiling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Degradation of human ATF6α was markedly delayed in EDEM1,3-DKO cells.
source: Accordingly, degradation of human ATF6α, a transmembrane-type gpERAD substrate, and mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA, a soluble gpERAD substrate, was markedly delayed in EDEM1, 3-DKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and 1F), similarly to the case of EDEM2-KO cells (Ninagawa et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: Degradation of mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA was markedly delayed in EDEM1,3-DKO cells.
source: Accordingly, degradation of human ATF6α, a transmembrane-type gpERAD substrate, and mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA, a soluble gpERAD substrate, was markedly delayed in EDEM1, 3-DKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and 1F), similarly to the case of EDEM2-KO cells (Ninagawa et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: EDEM1,3-DKO cells grew slightly more slowly than wild-type cells.
source: To evaluate their functionality in gpERAD, we constructed EDEM1, 3-double KO (DKO) cells (two independent clones #1 and #2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and S1B), which expressed neither EDEM1 mRNA nor EDEM3 mRNA (Figure 2B), and grew slightly more slowly than wild-type (WT) cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), as we previously described for the construction of EDEM1/2/3-triple KO (TKO) cells (Ninagawa et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by doubling time data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: EDEM3 produced M7A and M7C from M8B with no preference for the mannose residue in the A or C branch.
source: M7 turned out to be M7A and M7C (Figure 5D (a)), indicating no preference of EDEM3 toward the mannose residue present in the A or C branch of M8B.
evidence: Supported by HPLC isomer identification data shown in Figure 5D(a)

claim: M8B was converted to M7 only slightly by purified EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex, and M6 and M5 were hardly detected even after 24 hr incubation.
source: In contrast, M8B was converted to M7 only slightly by purified EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex, and M6 and M5 were hardly detected even after 24 hr incubation (Figure 5C), indicating a strong preference of EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex toward M9 (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 5C

claim: EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex has a strong preference toward M9.
source: In contrast, M8B was converted to M7 only slightly by purified EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex, and M6 and M5 were hardly detected even after 24 hr incubation (Figure 5C), indicating a strong preference of EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex toward M9 (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from poor activity on M8B and citation to previous work showing activity on M9

claim: The entire route of oligosaccharide processing in mammalian gpERAD has been established.
source: Based on these results, we have established the route of oligosaccharide processing in mammalian gpERAD (Figure 5E).
evidence: Inferred from combined experimental data on EDEM activities

claim: The route of oligosaccharide processing in mammalian gpERAD proceeds from M9 to M8B via EDEM2-TXNDC11, then from M8B to M7A, M7C, M6, and M5 via EDEM3/EDEM1.
source: Based on these results, we have established the route of oligosaccharide processing in mammalian gpERAD (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by combined experimental data and schematic shown in Figure 5E

claim: 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA purified from EDEM1,3-DKO cells possesses N-glycans of M8B.
source: 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA and ATF6α(C) tagged with 3xMyc were purified from EDEM1, 3-DKO cells overexpressing TAP-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA and ATF6(C) tagged with TAP2 (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), respectively, by transfection (Figure 6A (a) and 7A (a)). They were expected to possess N-glycans of M8B, which we confirmed by MS analysis (see top panel of Figure 6B (b) and Figure 7B (b)); it should be noted that each oligosaccharide was detected as two peaks consisting of [M + H]+, a proton adduct ion, and [M + Na]+, a sodium adduct ion.
evidence: Supported by MS analysis shown in Figure 6B(b)

claim: ATF6α(C) tagged with 3xMyc purified from EDEM1,3-DKO cells possesses N-glycans of M8B.
source: 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA and ATF6α(C) tagged with 3xMyc were purified from EDEM1, 3-DKO cells overexpressing TAP-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA and ATF6(C) tagged with TAP2 (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), respectively, by transfection (Figure 6A (a) and 7A (a)). They were expected to possess N-glycans of M8B, which we confirmed by MS analysis (see top panel of Figure 6B (b) and Figure 7B (b)); it should be noted that each oligosaccharide was detected as two peaks consisting of [M + H]+, a proton adduct ion, and [M + Na]+, a sodium adduct ion.
evidence: Supported by MS analysis shown in Figure 7B(b)

claim: 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA purified from EDEM1,3-DKO cells is completely sensitive to digestion with endoglycosidase H.
source: Indeed, they were completely sensitive to digestion with endoglycosidase H (Endo H) (Figure 6A (b) and 7 A (b)).
evidence: Supported by Endo H digestion data shown in Figure 6A(b)

claim: ATF6α(C) tagged with 3xMyc purified from EDEM1,3-DKO cells is completely sensitive to digestion with endoglycosidase H.
source: Indeed, they were completely sensitive to digestion with endoglycosidase H (Endo H) (Figure 6A (b) and 7 A (b)).
evidence: Supported by Endo H digestion data shown in Figure 7A(b)

claim: 6xMyc-tagged EDEM1 caused a downward shift to the band of 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA purified from EDEM1,3-DKO cells after incubation.
source: The band of 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA purified from transfected EDEM1, 3-DKO cells exhibited a downward shift after incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM1 (Figure 6B (a), lane 4) and EDEM3(Q543N) (lane 10) but not with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex (lane 7).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6B(a)

claim: 6xMyc-tagged EDEM3(Q543N) caused a downward shift to the band of 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA purified from EDEM1,3-DKO cells after incubation.
source: The band of 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA purified from transfected EDEM1, 3-DKO cells exhibited a downward shift after incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM1 (Figure 6B (a), lane 4) and EDEM3(Q543N) (lane 10) but not with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex (lane 7).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6B(a)

claim: 6xMyc-tagged EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex did not cause a downward shift to the band of 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA purified from EDEM1,3-DKO cells after incubation.
source: The band of 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA purified from transfected EDEM1, 3-DKO cells exhibited a downward shift after incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM1 (Figure 6B (a), lane 4) and EDEM3(Q543N) (lane 10) but not with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex (lane 7).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6B(a)

claim: M8B on 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA was converted to M5 almost completely after 24 hr incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM1.
source: MS analysis of 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA samples after 24 hr incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM1 and EDEM3(Q543N) revealed that M8B was converted to M5 almost completely, whereas a major peak was still M8B after 24 hr incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex (Figure 6B (b)).
evidence: Supported by MS analysis shown in Figure 6B(b)

claim: M8B on 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA was converted to M5 almost completely after 24 hr incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM3(Q543N).
source: MS analysis of 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA samples after 24 hr incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM1 and EDEM3(Q543N) revealed that M8B was converted to M5 almost completely, whereas a major peak was still M8B after 24 hr incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex (Figure 6B (b)).
evidence: Supported by MS analysis shown in Figure 6B(b)

claim: A major peak was still M8B after 24 hr incubation of 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex.
source: MS analysis of 6xMyc-tagged mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA samples after 24 hr incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM1 and EDEM3(Q543N) revealed that M8B was converted to M5 almost completely, whereas a major peak was still M8B after 24 hr incubation with 6xMyc-tagged EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex (Figure 6B (b)).
evidence: Supported by MS analysis shown in Figure 6B(b)

claim: EDEM3 and EDEM1 are more active on protein-bound M8B than on free M8B.
source: We concluded that EDEM3 and EDEM1 are more active on protein-bound M8B than on free M8B.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of activity on PA-M8B versus glycoprotein-bound M8B

claim: Coexpression of EDEM3 and ERp46 is likely to facilitate the formation of disulfide bonding between C82 and C441 of human EDEM3.
source: It was previously shown that the MHD of EDEM3 is transiently disulfide-bonded to the thioredoxin domain-containing protein ERp46, and that coexpression of EDEM3 and ERp46 enhances EDEM3 activity in gpERAD (Yu et al., 2018). Based on our current results, coexpression of EDEM3 and ERp46 is likely to facilitate the formation of disulfide bonding between C82 and C441 of human EDEM3 (C83 and C442 of mouse EDEM3) in the MHD, which is required for EDEM3 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity (Figure 2D).
evidence: Inferred from current mutagenesis data and previous work on ERp46 (Yu et al., 2018)

claim: Once fully folded with correct disulfide bonding in the MHD, EDEM3 requires no partner protein to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity in vitro.
source: Once fully folded with correct disulfide bonding in the MHD, EDEM3 requires no partner protein to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity in vitro, in contrast to EDEM2.
evidence: Inferred from successful purification and activity of EDEM3 alone

claim: EDEM2 requires a partner protein (TXNDC11) to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity in vitro.
source: Once fully folded with correct disulfide bonding in the MHD, EDEM3 requires no partner protein to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity in vitro, in contrast to EDEM2.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with EDEM3 and previous work

claim: The conformation of noncomplexed and complexed EDEM2 with TXNDC11 differs.
source: We previously showed that the conformation of noncomplexed and complexed EDEM2 with TXNDC11 differs, using sensitivity to trypsin digestion (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (George et al., 2020)

claim: The structure of the catalytic site of EDEM2 may become significantly different to that of EDEM1 or EDEM3 following intramolecular disulfide bond formation in the MHD plus intermolecular disulfide bonding between EDEM2 and TXNDC11.
source: It is possible that the structure of the catalytic site of EDEM2 becomes significantly different to that of EDEM1 or EDEM3 following intramolecular disulfide bond formation in the MHD plus intermolecular disulfide bonding between EDEM2 and TXNDC11; this may explain not only the specificity of EDEM2 toward M9 but also the requirement for TXNDC11 as a stable partner of EDEM2.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of structural differences

claim: Structural differences in EDEM2 may explain the specificity of EDEM2 toward M9 and the requirement for TXNDC11 as a stable partner.
source: It is possible that the structure of the catalytic site of EDEM2 becomes significantly different to that of EDEM1 or EDEM3 following intramolecular disulfide bond formation in the MHD plus intermolecular disulfide bonding between EDEM2 and TXNDC11; this may explain not only the specificity of EDEM2 toward M9 but also the requirement for TXNDC11 as a stable partner of EDEM2.
evidence: Speculative interpretation

claim: Sequential mannose trimming of N-glycan from M9 to M8B and then to oligosaccharides exposing the α1,6-linked mannosyl residue facilitates ER-associated degradation of misfolded glycoproteins.
source: Sequential mannose trimming of N-glycan, from M9 to M8B and then to oligosaccharides exposing the α1,6-linked mannosyl residue (M7A, M6, and M5), facilitates endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation of misfolded glycoproteins (gpERAD).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge in the field

claim: In yeast, the α1,2-mannosidases Mns1 and Htm1 carry out the first and second mannose trimming steps, respectively.
source: In yeast, the α1,2-mannosidases Mns1 and Htm1 carry out the first and second mannose trimming steps, respectively (Ninagawa et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to review (Ninagawa et al., 2021)

claim: EDEM2 is required for the conversion of M9 to M8B in human cells.
source: We have constructed knockout (KO) cells for α1,2-mannosidase candidate genes, namely EDEM1, EDEM2, and EDEM3 (Htm1 orthologues), in human HCT116 diploid cells, and have shown that EDEM2 is required for the conversion of M9 to M8B and that EDEM3 (mainly) and EDEM1 (partly) are required for the conversion of M8B to oligosaccharides, which exposes the α1,6-linked mannosyl residue (Ninagawa et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Ninagawa et al., 2014)

claim: EDEM3 (mainly) and EDEM1 (partly) are required for the conversion of M8B to oligosaccharides exposing the α1,6-linked mannosyl residue in human cells.
source: We have constructed knockout (KO) cells for α1,2-mannosidase candidate genes, namely EDEM1, EDEM2, and EDEM3 (Htm1 orthologues), in human HCT116 diploid cells, and have shown that EDEM2 is required for the conversion of M9 to M8B and that EDEM3 (mainly) and EDEM1 (partly) are required for the conversion of M8B to oligosaccharides, which exposes the α1,6-linked mannosyl residue (Ninagawa et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Ninagawa et al., 2014)

claim: EDEM2 alone exhibits no mannosidase activity toward M9.
source: Further, our recent biochemical analysis has clarified that although EDEM2 alone exhibits no mannosidase activity toward M9, as reported previously (Mast et al., 2005; Shenkman et al., 2018), EDEM2 stably disulfide-bonded to the thioredoxin domain-containing protein TXNDC11 catalyzes the first mannose trimming step from M9 to M8B in vitro (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Mast et al., 2005; Shenkman et al., 2018)

claim: EDEM2 stably disulfide-bonded to TXNDC11 catalyzes the first mannose trimming step from M9 to M8B in vitro.
source: Further, our recent biochemical analysis has clarified that although EDEM2 alone exhibits no mannosidase activity toward M9, as reported previously (Mast et al., 2005; Shenkman et al., 2018), EDEM2 stably disulfide-bonded to the thioredoxin domain-containing protein TXNDC11 catalyzes the first mannose trimming step from M9 to M8B in vitro (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (George et al., 2020)

claim: Intramolecular disulfide bond formation in the mannosidase homology domain is considered essential for EDEM2 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity.
source: Intramolecular disulfide bond formation in the mannosidase homology domain (MHD) is considered essential for EDEM2 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity because mutation of either C65 or C408 inactivated EDEM2 in gpERAD (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (George et al., 2020)

claim: Mutation of either C65 or C408 inactivated EDEM2 in gpERAD.
source: Intramolecular disulfide bond formation in the mannosidase homology domain (MHD) is considered essential for EDEM2 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity because mutation of either C65 or C408 inactivated EDEM2 in gpERAD (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (George et al., 2020)

claim: MAN1B1 can produce M6 and M5 from M9 in vitro.
source: We employed MAN1B1 as a control of an extensive α1,2-mannosidase, based on a report that it can produce M6 and M5 from M9 in vitro (Aikawa et al., 2012); we confirmed this observation (see Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Aikawa et al., 2012) and confirmed by data in Figure 5C

claim: Both TAP-tagged MAN1B1 and MAN1B1(Δ105) are active mannosidases.
source: Both TAP-tagged MAN1B1 and MAN1B1(Δ105) are active mannosidases, as their overexpression in EDEM2-KO cells caused a downward shift to the transfected mCD3-δ-ΔTM-HA band (Figure 4C (b)).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4C(b)

claim: M7C is present in small amounts on glycoproteins in HCT116 cells.
source: In addition, both EDEM3 and EDEM1 nearly equally produced M7A and M7C from M8B (Figure 5D (a)), which explains the presence of a small amount of M7C on glycoproteins in HCT116 cells (Ninagawa et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Ninagawa et al., 2014)

claim: M7C is likely converted to M6 and then to M5 by EDEM3 and EDEM1.
source: M7C is likely converted to M6 and then to M5 by EDEM3 and EDEM1, because they have no preference for the mannose residue in the A branch or C branch of M8B.
evidence: Inferred from lack of branch preference in M8B trimming

claim: The entire route of oligosaccharide processing and the enzymes responsible for it have been established for mammalian gpERAD for the first time.
source: Thus, the entire route of oligosaccharide processing and the enzymes responsible for it have been established for mammalian gpERAD for the first time (Figure 5E).
evidence: Inferred from combined experimental results

claim: The MHD of EDEM3 is transiently disulfide-bonded to the thioredoxin domain-containing protein ERp46.
source: It was previously shown that the MHD of EDEM3 is transiently disulfide-bonded to the thioredoxin domain-containing protein ERp46, and that coexpression of EDEM3 and ERp46 enhances EDEM3 activity in gpERAD (Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Yu et al., 2018)

claim: Coexpression of EDEM3 and ERp46 enhances EDEM3 activity in gpERAD.
source: It was previously shown that the MHD of EDEM3 is transiently disulfide-bonded to the thioredoxin domain-containing protein ERp46, and that coexpression of EDEM3 and ERp46 enhances EDEM3 activity in gpERAD (Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Yu et al., 2018)

claim: Disulfide bonding between C82 and C441 of human EDEM3 in the MHD is required for EDEM3 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity.
source: Based on our current results, coexpression of EDEM3 and ERp46 is likely to facilitate the formation of disulfide bonding between C82 and C441 of human EDEM3 (C83 and C442 of mouse EDEM3) in the MHD, which is required for EDEM3 to exhibit α1,2-mannosidase activity (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The α1,2-mannosidase MAN1B1 appears to play only a very minor role in gpERAD.
source: Our previous genetic analysis revealed that the α1,2-mannosidase MAN1B1 (a sole Mns1 orthologue) appears to play only a very minor role in gpERAD (Ninagawa et al., 2014), contrary to the original proposals (Avezov et al., 2008; Gonzalez et al., 1999; Hosokawa et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Ninagawa et al., 2014)

claim: Endogenous MAN1B1 is localized in the Golgi apparatus.
source: Our current results with another α1,2-mannosidase MAN1B1 (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) are well consistent with a previous report showing the Golgi localization of endogenous MAN1B1 by immunofluorescence (Pan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Pan et al., 2011)

claim: Introduction of 3xFlag-tagged EDEM2 into EDEM2-KO cells produced its monomer, and probably dimer and aggregated forms.
source: As we reported previously, analysis by non-reducing SDS-PAGE followed by immunoblotting showed that introduction of 3xFlag-tagged EDEM2 into EDEM2-KO cells produced its monomer, and probably dimer and aggregated forms, whereas simultaneous introduction of 3xFlag-tagged TXNDC11 and 3xFlag-tagged EDEM2 into EDEM2-KO cells produced a high molecular weight complex of EDEM2 and TXNDC11, designated EDEM2§–3xFlag (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by non-reducing SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Simultaneous introduction of 3xFlag-tagged TXNDC11 and 3xFlag-tagged EDEM2 into EDEM2-KO cells produced a high molecular weight complex of EDEM2 and TXNDC11.
source: As we reported previously, analysis by non-reducing SDS-PAGE followed by immunoblotting showed that introduction of 3xFlag-tagged EDEM2 into EDEM2-KO cells produced its monomer, and probably dimer and aggregated forms, whereas simultaneous introduction of 3xFlag-tagged TXNDC11 and 3xFlag-tagged EDEM2 into EDEM2-KO cells produced a high molecular weight complex of EDEM2 and TXNDC11, designated EDEM2§–3xFlag (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by non-reducing SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Both TXNDC11 and the EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex are detected as a doublet band due to alternative translational initiation of TXNDC11 at M1 or M58.
source: It should be noted that both TXNDC11 and the EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex are detected as a doublet band due to alternative translational initiation of TXNDC11 at M1 or M58 (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (George et al., 2020)

claim: TXNDC11(M1A) is expressed as both soluble and transmembrane proteins because its N-terminal hydrophobic region functions by chance as either a signal sequence or a transmembrane domain.
source: It should be noted that TXNDC11(M1A) was used to purify EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex; TXNDC11(M58A) is expressed only as a transmembrane protein, whereas TXNDC11(M1A) is expressed as both soluble and transmembrane proteins because its N-terminal hydrophobic region functions by chance as either a signal sequence or a transmembrane domain (TMD) (Figure 1B), allowing us to purify a soluble complex of EDEM2 and TXNDC11.
evidence: Inferred from structural features shown in Figure 1B

claim: TXNDC11(M58A) is expressed only as a transmembrane protein.
source: It should be noted that TXNDC11(M1A) was used to purify EDEM2-TXNDC11 complex; TXNDC11(M58A) is expressed only as a transmembrane protein, whereas TXNDC11(M1A) is expressed as both soluble and transmembrane proteins because its N-terminal hydrophobic region functions by chance as either a signal sequence or a transmembrane domain (TMD) (Figure 1B), allowing us to purify a soluble complex of EDEM2 and TXNDC11.
evidence: Inferred from structural features shown in Figure 1B

claim: C65 of human EDEM2 is conserved as C160 of human EDEM1 and C82 of human EDEM3.
source: C65 of human EDEM2 is conserved as C160 of human EDEM1 and C82 of human EDEM3, whereas C408 of human EDEM2 is conserved as C529 of human EDEM1 and C441 of human EDEM3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A

claim: C408 of human EDEM2 is conserved as C529 of human EDEM1 and C441 of human EDEM3.
source: C65 of human EDEM2 is conserved as C160 of human EDEM1 and C82 of human EDEM3, whereas C408 of human EDEM2 is conserved as C529 of human EDEM1 and C441 of human EDEM3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A

claim: EDEM1,3-DKO cells expressed neither EDEM1 mRNA nor EDEM3 mRNA.
source: To evaluate their functionality in gpERAD, we constructed EDEM1, 3-double KO (DKO) cells (two independent clones #1 and #2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and S1B), which expressed neither EDEM1 mRNA nor EDEM3 mRNA (Figure 2B), and grew slightly more slowly than wild-type (WT) cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), as we previously described for the construction of EDEM1/2/3-triple KO (TKO) cells (Ninagawa et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B

claim: M9 was accumulated in EDEM-TKO cells.
source: M9 was accumulated in EDEM-TKO cells as we described previously (Ninagawa et al., 2015), whereas M8B was accumulated in EDEM1, 3-DKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), as we expected.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Ninagawa et al., 2015)
